items.prompt: The reply-suggestions feature pays $3,200/month for a reserved GPU pool no matter how many suggestions get generated. What kind of cost is this?
choices: Variable cost
Fixed cost
Marginal revenue
Amortized cost
items.explanation: It doesn't change with volume — one suggestion or a million, the reservation bill is the same $3,200. That's the definition of a fixed cost.
items.reference:
Fixed

Same regardless of volume (GPU reservation)

Variable

Scales with volume ($0.011/suggestion)

Why: total cost = fixed + variable×units; mixing the two up breaks every downstream calculation.

items.prompt: The feature also pays $0.011 for every suggestion actually generated. What kind of cost is this?
choices: Fixed cost
Sunk cost
Variable cost
Opportunity cost
items.explanation: It scales directly with usage — twice as many suggestions, twice as much of this cost. That's a variable cost.
items.reference:
Fixed

Same regardless of volume (GPU reservation)

Variable

Scales with volume ($0.011/suggestion)

Why: total cost = fixed + variable×units; mixing the two up breaks every downstream calculation.

items.prompt: A team signs a 1-year, $12,000 contract for a transcription API, paid as a flat monthly $1,000 regardless of how many minutes get transcribed. Is the $1,000/month fixed or variable?
choices: Variable — it changes every month
Fixed — it's the same regardless of usage that month
Neither — contracts aren't costs
It's revenue, not cost
items.explanation: A flat monthly payment that doesn't depend on that month's usage is fixed, even though the underlying contract has a defined total size and end date.
items.reference:
Fixed

Same regardless of volume (GPU reservation)

Variable

Scales with volume ($0.011/suggestion)

Why: total cost = fixed + variable×units; mixing the two up breaks every downstream calculation.

items.prompt: Fixed cost is $2,000/month, variable cost is $0.02/unit, and 10,000 units are produced this month. What's the cost per unit?
items.explanation: $2,000 / 10,000 = $0.20 of fixed cost per unit, plus the $0.02 variable cost, for $0.22 total per unit.
items.reference:
costPerUnit = fixedCost / units + variableCostPerUnit

Why: spreading the fixed piece across more units is exactly what makes cost-per-unit fall as volume grows.

items.prompt: If the same $2,000 fixed cost is instead spread over 100,000 units (10x the volume, same variable rate of $0.02), what happens to cost per unit?
choices: It rises, because more units means more total cost
It falls, because the fixed cost is spread thinner
It stays exactly $0.22
It becomes undefined
items.explanation: $2,000 / 100,000 = $0.02 of fixed cost per unit now, plus $0.02 variable, for $0.04 total — noticeably lower than $0.22, because the same fixed cost is divided across far more units.
items.reference:
costPerUnit = fixedCost / units + variableCostPerUnit

Why: spreading the fixed piece across more units is exactly what makes cost-per-unit fall as volume grows.

items.prompt: What does "unit economics" mean, in the sense this unit uses it?
choices: Analyzing your company's total annual budget
Attaching real cost and revenue to one unit — one user, one request, one transaction
A pricing strategy where every product costs the same
An accounting standard for reporting fixed assets
items.explanation: Unit economics is specifically about the per-unit figure — cost and revenue for one user/request/transaction — rather than reasoning only about aggregate totals.

items.prompt: Why is "the cloud bill went up a bit this month" not the same kind of statement as unit economics?
choices: It's more precise than unit economics
It's an aggregate observation with no per-unit or per-segment breakdown
It only applies to free-tier users
Cloud bills are always fixed costs
items.explanation: An aggregate total tells you the bill moved, but not why, for whom, or per unit — exactly the detail that caught the free tier's loss in the scenario above.

items.prompt: A company-wide "cost per user" of about $0.41/month sounds harmless. What does that average actually hide, in the reply-suggestions scenario?
choices: Nothing — the average is always the correct number to look at
That the free tier alone is losing about $13,700/month, masked by blending in the profitable paid tier
That paid users are secretly unprofitable
That the GPU reservation is underpriced
items.explanation: Blending two very different segments into one average can make a real, segment-specific loss disappear into a small, unremarkable-looking number.
items.reference:
Blended average

≈$0.41/user company-wide — looks fine

Free tier alone

~$13,700/month loss — not fine

items.prompt: What's the fix for a misleading blended average like this?
choices: Report even fewer numbers, to avoid confusion
Compute cost and revenue per segment first, then blend if a company-wide figure is still needed
Always round the average up
Stop tracking cost per user entirely
items.explanation: Segment-level unit economics catches what a single blended figure hides — compute per segment first, blend second, not the other way around.

items.prompt: A one-time $9,600 migration cost is paid entirely in month 1 of a 12-month contract. What problem does amortizing it solve?
choices: It makes the total cost smaller
It spreads the cost evenly across the 12 months it actually covers, instead of distorting month 1
It converts the cost from variable to fixed
It removes the cost from the books entirely
items.explanation: Amortization spreads a lump-sum cost across the period it belongs to, so no single month's numbers are skewed by when the invoice happened to be paid.

items.prompt: Without amortizing the $9,600 migration cost, what would month 1's unit economics look like compared to month 2's?
choices: Identical, since the cost is the same contract either way
Month 1 would look far worse — carrying the whole $9,600 — while month 2 onward would look artificially cheap
Month 2 would look worse instead
There would be no difference to unit economics, only to accounting
items.explanation: Expensing the full amount in month 1 spikes that month's per-unit cost and makes every later month look better than it really is by comparison.

items.prompt: What does "break-even" mean for a feature or product?
choices: The point where the team stops working on it
The volume at which total revenue equals total cost
The month the contract expires
The moment fixed cost reaches zero
items.explanation: Break-even is a volume, not a date or a feeling — it's specifically where cumulative revenue and cumulative cost are equal.
items.reference:
breakEvenUnits = fixedCost / (price − variableCost)

Why: that's the volume at which cumulative revenue first catches up to cumulative cost.

items.prompt: The free tier charges $0/month. What does that imply about its break-even point?
choices: It breaks even instantly, since there's nothing to pay for
There is no finite break-even volume — revenue never catches up to cost at any volume
Break-even doesn't apply to free products
It breaks even once 40,000 users sign up
items.explanation: With $0 revenue per unit, revenue can never equal a positive cost at any volume — the break-even point is effectively infinite.
items.reference:
breakEvenUnits = fixedCost / (price − variableCost)

Why: that's the volume at which cumulative revenue first catches up to cumulative cost.

items.prompt: Fixed cost is allocated evenly across all 48,000 users instead of being isolated per segment. What does that even split do to the free tier's apparent unit economics?
choices: Makes them look worse than reality
Makes them look better than reality, by handing the free tier a smaller fixed-cost share than its usage would justify
Has no effect on the reported numbers
Converts the free tier's cost into revenue
items.explanation: An even-by-user split under-charges a heavy-usage segment (like the free tier here, which drives a large share of total generations) relative to its actual footprint, making it look cheaper than it is.
items.reference:
AllocationFree-tier fixed share
Even, by users$3,200 × 40000/48000 ≈ $2,667
By usage share$3,200 × 1,000,000/1,480,000 ≈ $2,162

Why: the allocation method you pick changes the reported number, even though total company-wide cost stays the same either way.

items.prompt: If fixed cost were instead allocated by usage share (each segment pays proportional to its share of total suggestions generated, not its share of users), what happens to the free tier's reported cost, given it generates 1,000,000 of the 1,480,000 total monthly suggestions?
choices: It falls, since usage share (67.6%) is lower than the free tier's user share (83.3%)
It stays exactly the same as the even-by-user allocation
It rises, since usage share is higher than user share
Usage share can't be used for allocation
items.explanation: The free tier is 40,000 of 48,000 users (83.3%) but only 1,000,000 of 1,480,000 suggestions (67.6%) — a usage-based allocation gives it a smaller fixed-cost share than an even-by-user split would.
items.reference:

Why: the allocation method you pick changes the reported number, even though total company-wide cost stays the same either way.

items.prompt: Does total company-wide cost change depending on which allocation method (by users vs. by usage) is used to split the $3,200 fixed cost between segments?
choices: Yes, usage-based allocation makes the total bill smaller
No — total cost is fixed at $19,480 either way; only how it's attributed between segments changes
Yes, but only if variable cost also changes
No allocation method changes anything about the numbers
items.explanation: Allocation only decides how a fixed pool of cost is attributed across segments for reporting purposes — it never changes the actual total the company pays.

items.prompt: Why does cost per unit generally fall as volume grows, all else equal?
choices: Vendors always discount at higher volume
The fixed cost gets divided across more units, shrinking its per-unit share
Variable cost per unit falls automatically at scale
It doesn't — cost per unit is constant by definition
items.explanation: Cost per unit is fixed/units + variable — as units grows, the fixed/units term shrinks, pulling the total down even if the variable rate never changes.

items.prompt: The chart in L2 shows cost-per-suggestion rising again around 2,000K suggestions/month before falling once more. What does that bump most likely represent?
choices: A billing error
A new, larger fixed-cost tier (e.g. a second GPU reservation) kicking in to handle the higher volume
Variable cost per unit suddenly increasing
The free tier being removed
items.explanation: Cost-per-unit isn't a smooth curve in practice — it's a staircase, because fixed costs come in discrete tiers that step up once volume outgrows the current one.

items.prompt: What is contribution margin?
choices: Fixed cost divided by units
Price per unit minus variable cost per unit
Total revenue minus total cost
Fixed cost minus variable cost
items.explanation: Contribution margin is what's left of one unit's revenue after only its variable cost — before fixed cost is even considered.

items.prompt: A paid user pays $12/month and generates 60 suggestions at $0.011 each ($0.66 total variable cost). What's that user's contribution margin?
items.explanation: $12.00 − $0.66 = $11.34 — nearly all of the $12 survives as contribution margin, since the variable cost per user is small relative to price.

items.prompt: Which formula correctly computes break-even units?
choices: fixedCost × contributionMargin
fixedCost / contributionMargin
contributionMargin / fixedCost
fixedCost − contributionMargin
items.explanation: Break-even units is fixed cost divided by contribution margin — how many units' worth of margin it takes to cover the fixed cost.

items.prompt: Using $3,200 fixed cost and an $11.34 per-paid-user contribution margin, roughly how many paid users are needed to break even?
choices: About 28
About 282
About 2,820
About 3,200
items.explanation: 3,200 / 11.34 ≈ 282.2 — since the paid tier already has 8,000 users, it's comfortably past break-even.

items.prompt: What does a full amortization schedule show that a single "$800/month" figure doesn't?
choices: Nothing extra — they're the same information
The month-by-month amount, cumulative total, and remaining balance over the whole period
The vendor's original invoice number
Only the final month's cost
items.explanation: A schedule tracks the running cumulative and remaining balance month by month — useful for reconciling against a finance report, not just knowing the flat monthly rate.

items.prompt: In a straight-line amortization schedule for a $9,600 cost over 12 months, what should the "remaining" value be after month 12?
choices: Undefined
items.explanation: By the final month, the full $9,600 has been recognized — remaining balance drops to exactly $0.

items.prompt: A free-tier user generates 25 suggestions/month at $0.011 each, paying $0. What is that user's contribution margin?
items.explanation: $0 (price) − $0.275 (25 × $0.011 variable cost) = -$0.275 — negative from the start, before fixed cost is even added.

items.prompt: If a segment's contribution margin per unit is negative, what does more volume in that segment do to total loss?
choices: Reduces it, since fixed cost gets spread thinner
Increases it — each additional unit adds more variable cost than revenue, on top of any fixed share
Has no effect on loss
Converts the segment to profitable once it's large enough
items.explanation: With negative contribution margin, every additional unit loses money on its own variable cost alone — growing that segment makes total loss larger, not smaller.

items.prompt: Write costPerUnit(fixedCost, variableCostPerUnit, units) that returns fixed cost spread across units plus the variable cost per unit. It should throw if units is 0 or negative.

tests.description: combines fixed share and variable cost
matches the reply-suggestions free-tier-style numbers
throws on zero units

items.explanation: Dividing fixedCost by units gives the per-unit share of the fixed cost; adding variableCostPerUnit accounts for the part of cost that scales with volume. The guard clause turns an undefined division (fixed/0) into an explicit, catchable error instead of a silent Infinity that would corrupt any calculation built on top of it.
items.reference:
costPerUnit = fixed/units + variable

Why: a zero-unit guard clause matters — dividing by zero would otherwise silently produce Infinity/NaN and corrupt everything downstream.

items.prompt: Write costPerUnit(fixedCost, variableCostPerUnit, units) that returns fixed cost spread across units plus the variable cost per unit. It should throw if units is 0 or negative.

tests.description: spreads a larger fixed cost over a larger volume
same fixed cost over 10x the units is cheaper per unit
throws on negative units

items.explanation: The fixed/units term shrinks as units grows, which is exactly the economies-of-scale effect from L2 — the same function that computes cost-per-unit also proves that relationship for any inputs, not just the two numbers in the chart.
items.reference:
costPerUnit = fixed/units + variable

Why: a zero-unit guard clause matters — dividing by zero would otherwise silently produce Infinity/NaN and corrupt everything downstream.

items.prompt: Write amortizationSchedule(totalCost, months) returning an array of { month, amount, cumulative, remaining } straight-line rows, one per month, evenly spreading totalCost.

tests.description: one row per month
first row splits the cost evenly
last row's remaining balance is exactly zero

items.explanation: Dividing totalCost by months once gives the flat per-month amount; the loop just accumulates it and tracks what's left. For an evenly-divisible total like $1,200/12, no rounding remainder needs special handling, so remaining reaches exactly $0 on the final row.
items.reference:
Each row: month, amount, cumulative, remaining — remaining should hit exactly $0 on the last row.

Why: a schedule is what turns "$800/month" into something a finance review can actually reconcile against.

items.prompt: Write amortizationSchedule(totalCost, months) returning an array of { month, amount, cumulative, remaining } straight-line rows, one per month, evenly spreading totalCost.

tests.description: handles a shorter schedule
cumulative after month 2 is half the total
remaining after month 1 equals totalCost minus that month's amount

items.explanation: Each row's remaining balance is just totalCost minus however much has been recognized so far — it should decrease monotonically to zero, which is a useful sanity check on any schedule implementation.
items.reference:
Each row: month, amount, cumulative, remaining — remaining should hit exactly $0 on the last row.

Why: a schedule is what turns "$800/month" into something a finance review can actually reconcile against.

items.prompt: Write breakEvenUnits(fixedCost, pricePerUnit, variableCostPerUnit). Return Infinity if contribution margin is zero or negative, instead of throwing or dividing by a non-positive number.

tests.description: computes a normal break-even volume
zero margin returns Infinity
negative margin (free tier style) returns Infinity

items.explanation: Contribution margin (price minus variable cost) has to be strictly positive for any finite volume to recover the fixed cost — returning Infinity for zero or negative margin represents that reality ("no volume fixes this") instead of throwing an error that would need special-casing at every call site.
items.reference:
breakEvenUnits = fixedCost / (price − variableCost), or Infinity if margin ≤ 0

Why: a free tier's break-even is genuinely infinite, not a bug to special-case away.

items.prompt: Write breakEvenUnits(fixedCost, pricePerUnit, variableCostPerUnit). Return Infinity if contribution margin is zero or negative, instead of throwing or dividing by a non-positive number.

tests.description: matches the paid-tier numbers approximately
a healthy margin gives a smaller break-even than a thin one
larger fixed cost raises break-even, all else equal

items.explanation: Break-even scales inversely with contribution margin (a thinner margin needs more units to cover the same fixed cost) and directly with fixed cost (a bigger fixed cost needs more units too) — both relationships fall straight out of fixedCost / margin.
items.reference:
breakEvenUnits = fixedCost / (price − variableCost), or Infinity if margin ≤ 0

Why: a free tier's break-even is genuinely infinite, not a bug to special-case away.

items.prompt: Write marginPercent(revenue, cost) returning profit as a percentage of revenue. Handle revenue of 0: return 0 if cost is also 0, otherwise -Infinity.

tests.description: computes a normal margin percentage
zero revenue and zero cost is a 0% margin, not an error
zero revenue with positive cost is -Infinity

items.explanation: The standard formula (revenue - cost) / revenue * 100 divides by zero when revenue is zero, so that case needs an explicit branch — a free tier with real cost and zero revenue genuinely has an unbounded negative margin, which -Infinity represents honestly instead of throwing or returning a misleading 0.

items.prompt: Write marginPercent(revenue, cost) returning profit as a percentage of revenue. Handle revenue of 0: return 0 if cost is also 0, otherwise -Infinity.

tests.description: matches the paid-tier numbers approximately
a higher-margin segment returns a larger percentage
revenue exactly equal to cost is a 0% margin

items.explanation: Margin percent is comparable across segments of very different absolute size precisely because it normalizes by revenue — a small segment and a huge one can be compared fairly on this number even though their dollar totals aren't directly comparable.

items.prompt: Write allocateFixedCostByUsers(fixedCost, segmentUsers, totalUsers), splitting a shared fixed cost proportionally by each segment's share of total users.

tests.description: an even quarter split
a segment with no users gets no allocation
a segment with all the users gets the full fixed cost

items.explanation: This is just a proportional split — the segment's share of total users, applied to the fixed cost pool. It's a modeling choice, not the only correct one: allocating by usage share instead (see L3's extension question) can tell a meaningfully different per-segment story from the exact same total cost.
items.reference:
allocateFixedCostByUsers = fixedCost × (segmentUsers / totalUsers)

Why: the allocation basis (users vs. usage) changes the reported per-segment number without changing total company-wide cost.

items.prompt: Write allocateFixedCostByUsers(fixedCost, segmentUsers, totalUsers), splitting a shared fixed cost proportionally by each segment's share of total users.

tests.description: matches the free tier's fixed-cost share from the scenario
matches the paid tier's fixed-cost share from the scenario
the two segments' shares sum back to the full fixed cost

items.explanation: Because the two segments' user-share fractions always sum to 1, their allocated shares always sum back to the original fixed cost exactly — allocation redistributes cost, it never creates or destroys it, which is a useful invariant to test for.
items.reference:
allocateFixedCostByUsers = fixedCost × (segmentUsers / totalUsers)

Why: the allocation basis (users vs. usage) changes the reported per-segment number without changing total company-wide cost.

items.prompt: Write allocateFixedCostByUsers(fixedCost, segmentUsers, totalUsers), splitting a shared fixed cost proportionally by each segment's share of total users.

tests.description: a small segment gets a proportionally small share
doubling a segment's users roughly doubles its allocated share
allocation is linear in segmentUsers

items.explanation: Because the formula is linear in segmentUsers, doubling a segment's user count (with totalUsers held fixed) exactly doubles its allocated fixed-cost share — a handy property to sanity-check any allocation implementation against.
items.reference:
allocateFixedCostByUsers = fixedCost × (segmentUsers / totalUsers)

Why: the allocation basis (users vs. usage) changes the reported per-segment number without changing total company-wide cost.

items.prompt: breakEvenUnits returns Infinity instead of throwing when contribution margin is zero or negative. What's the advantage of Infinity over throwing an error here?
choices: Infinity is faster to compute than throwing
Infinity is a valid, comparable number (e.g. "is this break-even lower than that one?" still works) instead of forcing every caller to wrap the call in a try/catch
JavaScript doesn't support throwing from functions
There's no real advantage — throwing would be equally good
items.explanation: A caller comparing break-even points across segments, or plotting them, can treat Infinity like any other number in a comparison or a chart's domain — an exception would force special-case handling at every call site instead of letting the value flow through normally.

items.prompt: In the amortizationSchedule function, why does rounding matter more for real dollar amounts than it might seem from the math alone?
choices: It doesn't matter — floating point is always exact for money
Because floating-point division can leave tiny rounding errors that compound across many rows, so the last row often needs to absorb the remainder to land on exactly $0 remaining
Because JavaScript doesn't support decimal numbers
Because finance departments require whole-dollar amounts only
items.explanation: Repeatedly adding a rounded monthly amount can drift a cent or two off the true total by the final row — a robust schedule either accepts that small drift or explicitly makes the last row absorb whatever remainder is left, so the schedule sums to exactly the original total.

items.prompt: Why does costPerUnit throw on zero units instead of just letting the division happen?
choices: JavaScript throws automatically on any division by zero
A silent Infinity or NaN result would flow into every downstream calculation (segment cost, break-even, margin) without any clear signal that something upstream was wrong
Throwing makes the function run faster
Zero units is mathematically impossible to represent
items.explanation: JavaScript's `x / 0` returns Infinity rather than throwing, so without an explicit guard, a zero-volume segment would silently produce a nonsensical cost-per-unit that corrupts every later step instead of failing loudly at the source of the problem.
